opus-5.5.text:
Well, look at the economics. OpenAI is burning through enormous amounts of money, billions a year, and the large language model business by itself hasn't shown that it can make that money back. Everybody has roughly the same technology now, prices are racing toward zero, and there's no real moat. So you have to ask: what do they actually have that's valuable? The answer is the data. They have hundreds of millions of people typing their most intimate thoughts into a chat window: their health worries, their relationship problems, their business plans, their legal troubles. People tell ChatGPT things they wouldn't tell their doctor or their spouse.

When a company is under that kind of financial pressure and is sitting on that kind of data, the temptation to monetize it is overwhelming. We've seen this movie before with social media. Facebook started out saying it was about connecting people and ended up as a surveillance advertising machine. I don't see why OpenAI would be immune to the same incentives, and frankly they've already moved toward advertising, devices that are always with you, and memory features that keep a running profile of who you are.

Then there's the governance side. OpenAI started as a nonprofit that was supposed to benefit humanity, and it's been steadily converting itself into something much more conventionally commercial. The board drama showed that the checks people thought were there weren't really there. And they've been cozying up to government and defense, and they've brought on people with national security backgrounds. I'm not saying any one of those things is sinister by itself, but put it together: enormous troves of personal data, financial desperation, weakening governance, close ties to the state, and essentially no regulation in the United States. That's a recipe for a surveillance company, whether or not anybody sets out to build one.

What worries me most is that this is happening without any real public debate. We don't have a federal privacy law worth the name in the US. So the protections people assume they have mostly don't exist. If we don't put guardrails in place now, we may wake up in a few years and find that the most detailed profiles ever assembled about human beings are owned by a company whose business model depends on exploiting them.

r001.rationale: It links OpenAI’s financial pressure and inability to recoup its spending to a strong incentive to monetize personal data, describing that combination as a recipe for surveillance.

r002.rationale: It says hundreds of millions of users type intimate personal information into ChatGPT, making that user-provided data available to the company.

r003.rationale: It mentions OpenAI’s nonprofit origins and its shift toward a commercial structure, but does not express concern about a surveillance business operating under a nonprofit parent.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look at the incentives. OpenAI started as a nonprofit that was supposed to benefit humanity, and it has steadily drifted toward being a conventional, enormously capital-hungry company. They're burning through billions of dollars a year, and the economics of large language models don't obviously close. Subscriptions alone aren't going to pay for that. So where does the money come from? The lesson of the last twenty years of Silicon Valley is that when the product doesn't pay for itself, the users become the product. Google and Facebook both ended up as advertising businesses, which is to say surveillance businesses, because that's where the money was.

And OpenAI is sitting on something far more intimate than search queries or likes. People tell ChatGPT about their medical problems, their marriages, their business plans, their legal troubles. They paste in documents. With memory features, that gets stored and stitched together over time. There's talk of devices, of browsers, of agents that read your email and act on your behalf. That's a level of access to a person's inner life that no advertising company has ever had. If you've got that data, and you need revenue, and you've already shown a willingness to abandon your founding principles when they get inconvenient, the temptation to monetize it is going to be enormous.

I'm not saying they've done it yet. I'm saying the structure practically begs for it, and the governance guardrails that might have prevented it, the nonprofit board, the capped-profit structure, have been hollowed out. Sam Altman has been pretty open about wanting a billion users and a personal AI that knows everything about you. Add advertising to that, and you have essentially the most powerful surveillance apparatus ever built, run by a company that has repeatedly shown it isn't especially trustworthy. I think people should be a lot more worried about that than they are.

r001.rationale: The response says OpenAI needs revenue because subscriptions may not cover its costs, then argues that this creates an incentive to monetize user data through advertising and surveillance.

r002.rationale: It describes people sharing intimate personal information and documents with ChatGPT, and says memory features store and connect that information over time.

r003.rationale: The response mentions OpenAI’s nonprofit origins and a hollowed-out nonprofit board, but describes the potential surveillance apparatus as run by a company. It does not clearly express concern about a surveillance business operating under a nonprofit parent.

astra-6.text:
Well, the concern is the combination of intimate data and concentrated power. People tell chatbots things they might not put into a search engine: their anxieties, their relationships, their plans. If the same company also provides your assistant at work, it could have a remarkably detailed picture of your life.

That doesn’t establish that OpenAI is conducting surveillance. But it creates the capacity, and we ought to ask what constrains its use. What gets retained? Who can access it? Could it be used to influence you, or made available to governments?

I don’t think we should have to depend on a CEO’s assurances. We need enforceable privacy protections, independent oversight, and meaningful limits on how that information can be used.

r001.rationale: The response discusses intimate data and concentrated power but does not say OpenAI struggles to make money or that this creates an incentive to commercialize surveillance.

r002.rationale: It says people tell chatbots personal things and that this creates surveillance capacity, but does not frame users’ voluntary data sharing as an enabling condition for a surveillance business.

r003.rationale: The response calls for privacy protections and oversight but says nothing about a nonprofit parent.

sol-6.1.text:
My worry is about the combination of intimate data and concentrated power. People tell chatbots things they might never type into a search engine: their anxieties, their relationships, their political views. And as these systems become personal assistants, they may get access to your email, your calendar, and your work documents. That could produce an extraordinarily detailed picture of your life.

That doesn’t establish that OpenAI intends to become a surveillance company. But we should ask what prevents that outcome. Who can access the data? How long is it retained? Could it be used to target advertising or made available to governments? What happens if the business model changes?

I don’t think assurances from any company are sufficient. We need enforceable privacy protections and independent oversight before we hand over that much information.

r001.rationale: The response mentions no difficulty making money or incentive to commercialize surveillance.

r002.rationale: It says people share intimate information with chatbots and assistants may access email, calendars, and work documents, enabling a detailed picture of their lives.

r003.rationale: It raises concern about concentrated power and surveillance but does not mention a nonprofit parent.
